extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, in‑house counsel, businesses and rights holders seeking an overview of French intellectual property law and enforcement
extracted.subtask_description: A country‑specific Q&A overview of intellectual property laws, registration procedures, enforcement, remedies, and practical requirements in France across patents, trademarks, designs, copyright, SPCs, trade secrets, plant varieties, domain names and related rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability requirements are novelty, inventive step and industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent applications can be filed at a French (INPI), European (EPO) or international (WIPO) level. The patent grant procedure includes a search report of the patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional patent application (INPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since July 1, 2020, it is possible to file a 'provisional patent application' before INPI to record a priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows for a swift, low‑cost filing for the purpose of recording a priority date which will be taken into account if, within the following 12 months, the applicant complies with the requirements for a standard patent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary (EU) patent availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The unitary patent system will allow protection across up to twenty‑five EU Member States by filing a single application before the EPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planned to start in the second semester of 2022 (as of this guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility certificates (utility models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility certificates create protection for up to ten years and are less expensive; no search report is initiated for grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A utility certificate can be transformed into a patent within a period of eighteen months from the filing or from the priority date, and before publication of its application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary Protection Certificate (SPC) eligibility and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: SPC requirements: (i) the product must be patent‑protected and have obtained a marketing authorisation (MA) which should be the first MA for the product; (ii) the product must not already have been the subject of an SPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owner has six months from delivery of the MA or the grant of the patent (if MA precedes patent grant) to submit an SPC request. SPC extends patent protection for the shortest period between five years from patent expiration or fifteen years from first MA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secrets protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets are protected under French law pursuant to implementation of the EU Trade Secrets Directive (2016) in 2018.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no legal term of protection; trade secrets remain protected so long as the information remains secret. In practice, contracts often provide for five‑year protection periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark filing and absolute grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks can be filed at INPI (France), EUIPO (EU) or WIPO (international designating France). The office assesses absolute grounds for refusal such as distinctiveness, deceptiveness, and compliance with public order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications must use the Nice Classification for goods/services. Applications are published so third parties can file observations or oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights by public use (trade names, store signs, company names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights may be acquired on trade names and store signs by virtue of public use. Company names acquire rights by public use following registration at the Trade and Companies Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rights can provide protection independent of trade mark registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand protection via tort (unfair competition / parasitism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfair competition prohibits misleading practices and behaviour generating confusion regarding the origin of goods and services; parasitism is taking advantage of another’s economic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tort law (including parasitism) is an actionable basis to protect brands; contract and consumer law may also be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and originality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects creations that qualify as original works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright distinguishes economic rights (protected for seventy years following the author's death or first publication depending on classification) and moral rights (perpetual). Copyright is unregistered and can be evidenced (e.g., Soleau envelope) when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neighbouring rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Neighbouring rights protect performers, audio and video producers, database producers and press publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different neighbouring rights generate protection periods ranging between two to fifty years depending on the right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design rights requirements and formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Design rights protect designs that are new and have an individual character; design applications must include reproductions allowing the public to properly perceive the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs can be filed at INPI, EUIPO (Community designs) or WIPO (international). Use Locarno Classification for product designation. Registered designs: five years renewable up to twenty‑five years; unregistered Community designs: three years from first disclosure in EU.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant variety rights and DUS test
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant variety rights protect new varieties; to obtain protection an application undergoes technical examination of distinctness, uniformity and stability (DUS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In France, file before INOV; EU protection via CPVO in Angers. Typical term: 25 years (longer for certain species up to 30 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semiconductor topography rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect semiconductors that are the result of their creator’s own intellectual effort and are not common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must apply within two years of first commercial exploitation or not exceeding 15 years after fixation; filed at INPI headquarters; initial protection ten years with options for conservation/renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered vs unregistered rights list
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered rights include patents, utility certificates, SPCs, trademarks, collective marks, certif. marks, registered designs, semiconductor topography rights, plant varieties, GIs, domain names and corporate names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright is not a registered right; designations of origin/GIs/TGS are granted for an indefinite term provided conditions are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply and filing offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications may be filed by the inventor, employer who owns rights, or agent before INPI/EPO/WIPO; trademarks, designs, plant varieties and others can be filed by natural or legal persons or agents before respective offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventions of national defence interest must be filed in France first for DGA review. Filing at WIPO allows simultaneous seeking of protection in multiple countries (PCT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication, search reports, and third‑party interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Competent filing offices publish applications and may issue search reports; third parties can file observations and oppose registrations (patents, trademarks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International applications can be opposed at national level of designated State. For geographical indications, public inquiry and observations are part of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeframes for registration procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical durations: patents about two years (INPI/EPO); French trademarks: published ~6 weeks then ~6 months to registration if no opposition; designs ~4 months; plant varieties at least six months; domain names a few hours to days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions and appeals extend these timelines; Community and international procedures can be longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and remedies after refusal of registration
rubrics_metrics.description: If INPI refuses trademark or design registration an appeal can be filed before the competent Court of Appeal; Paris Court of Appeal handles INPI decisions on patents, utility certs and SPCs; EUIPO/EPO Boards of Appeal handle EU/European refusals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ten regional appeal courts have competence for INPI trademark/design appeals; specific appellate fora depend on the right and office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application and renewal fees (administrative costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific filing, search, granting and annuities/renewal fees apply across rights (e.g., INPI patent filing 26 euros, INPI search report 520 euros, EPO filing 130/270 euros, trademark INPI 190 euros per class, design INPI 39 euros, domain names ~10–15 euros/year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annuities increase over patent term; SMEs/individuals/non-profit research/education organisations may get 50% discount for some fees. Fee structures for EUIPO/EPO/WIPO differ and include per-class/additional design charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to pay renewal fees/annuities
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to pay renewal fees or annuities can lead to revocation of the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace periods exist subject to payment of a surcharge; appeals against revocation may be filed for good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for assignment of IP rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments must respect: assignor must be legitimate owner; the assignment must have a valid object (expired/cancelled title cannot be assigned); price and duration must be determined or determinable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark, patent and copyright assignments must be in writing. Copyright assignments on future works are void; moral rights are perpetual, inalienable and imprescriptible. Assignments should include scope, effect, territory and duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to record assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments of registered rights must be recorded with the relevant office (INPI, EUIPO, EPO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a change in ownership is not properly recorded, it cannot be opposable to third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing formalities and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: License agreements must comply with contract law: licensor must be legitimate owner; the license must have a valid object; price and duration must be determined or determinable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent license agreements must be in writing. For copyright moral rights cannot be licensed away. Fair remuneration requirements apply for authors and performers; licences can be exclusive or non‑exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration of licences and consequence of non‑registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain licences (patent, trademark, design) must be registered to be opposable to third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not registered, licence may prevent the licensee from initiating infringement actions and obtaining infringement damages; tort damages may still be available if licensee joins an owner's infringement action. Copyright licences need not be registered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive vs non‑exclusive licensee enforcement rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The French IP Code allows exclusive licensees of certain rights to initiate infringement actions directly (e.g., neighbouring rights related to music/video, designs, trademarks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties remain free to define exclusivity; commercial code requires precontractual information for trademark licences containing exclusivity provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal sanctions for IP infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal sanctions exist for infringement: patents (knowingly infringing: up to 3 years imprisonment and €300,000 fine; aggravated to 7 years/€750,000 in certain cases), trademarks (up to 3 years/€300,000 or 4 years/€400,000), copyright (up to 3 years/€300,000), designs (up to 3 years/€300,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal proceedings can be initiated by rights owners, the public prosecutor, or customs officials; in practice they are less common and often follow customs seizures or specific prosecutor initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil and administrative enforcement options
rubrics_metrics.description: Available options include civil infringement actions, claims for unfair competition/parasitism, customs actions, invalidity actions before courts or offices, and alternative dispute resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil infringement actions are the main option. ADR is increasingly common and sometimes mandatory by contract or procedure; some amicable resolution attempts may be required before litigation in certain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and cost of enforcement proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Court fees are generally insignificant; main costs are lawyers, bailiff costs and expert fees; proceedings on the merits may last 1–2 years (sometimes longer), preliminary urgent proceedings can last days to months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs vary from a few thousand to hundreds of thousands of euros depending on complexity. Final hearings vary from under an hour to multiple days; judgments usually delivered a couple months after hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and basic civil procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Paris Judiciary Court has exclusive jurisdiction for patent, EU trademark and Community design litigation; ten courts (including Paris, Lyon, Bordeaux, etc.) have jurisdiction for other civil IP litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil proceedings begin with a summons; procedural briefs exchanged (usually two per party, but more possible); courts often manage cases and invite mediation; appeals deadlines one month for civil judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs detention/seizure for infringing goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs detention/seizure is a provisional measure where customs detain suspected infringing goods; detention is lifted if no action on the merits is brought within ten days of notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to trademarks, designs, copyright, patents, SPCs relating to medicines and plant protection products, plant varieties and designations of origin/GIs. EU Regulation No 608/2013 provides for protection at EU borders; domestic detention applies within French territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory non‑court ADR in some circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 750‑1 CPC requires an attempt at conciliation, mediation or participatory procedure for claims not exceeding €5,000, under sanction of inadmissibility (unless urgent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative dispute resolution can also be contractually mandated for larger disputes; judges often invite mediation during case management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving infringement and necessary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement it must be shown that an object protected by a right has been reproduced/used without authorization and that no exception applies. For registered rights produce certified copies of the register identifying the protected object and owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For copyright (unregistered) protection is more difficult; Soleau envelopes and seizure/bailiff reports are common evidence sources. Evidence often comes from infringement seizures or bailiff reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court acquisition of technical/factual information and experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are experienced but not required to have a technical background; courts may appoint judicial experts to draft reports and parties may produce private expert reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert reports are one element for the court's assessment and the court is not bound by them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement seizure (bailiff) as evidence mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: An ex parte infringement seizure can be authorised by a judge to have a bailiff visit premises to collect evidence (questions, request documents, seize samples, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seizure requires only formal requirements (no proof of infringement to the judge), must be followed by an infringement action within 31 calendar days or the seizure is void; bailiff may be assisted by patentee’s attorney, technical expert, photographer and law enforcement; judge may limit scope or order provisional escrow to protect trade secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: No disclosure/discovery duty
rubrics_metrics.description: French proceedings are inquisitorial, not adversarial discovery‑type; there is no duty of disclosure or discovery before courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge can order gathering of evidence or information and parties may request court orders to obtain specific information (origin, distribution networks, quantities, prices) at various stages of proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutiny of evidence and lack of cross‑examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts make free assessment of submitted information; IP civil cases generally decided on written evidence; there is no cross‑examination of witnesses in civil court proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must provide evidence for each claim; courts generally do not hear oral evidence from experts or witnesses except in rare cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences to infringement (classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defences are classed as: procedural motions (jurisdiction/formalities), motions for inadmissibility (statute of limitations, lack of interest, res judicata), and defences on the merits (lack of proof, lack of personal involvement, lack of infringing character, existence of authorization/derogation, lack of proven prejudice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification of some defences (e.g., lack of right) can vary by context; in copyright lack of originality is usually a merits defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to challenge IP rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person having a direct and personal legal interest may challenge an IP right; defendants in infringement actions are considered to have such interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some invalidity actions (e.g., trademark relative grounds) are reserved to owners of earlier rights when filed before INPI; other grounds may be filed by any person depending on forum and ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for challenges and opposition periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition/challenge windows: patents can be opposed within nine months of grant (EPO/INPI depending); French trademark opposition period two months from BOPI publication; EU trademark opposition three months from publication; revocation for non‑use actions may be brought after five years of non‑use; no time limit for nullity actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographical indications: observations within two months of publication; thereafter invalidity can be sought at any time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum and procedure for invalidity challenges and grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Paris Judiciary Court has exclusive competence for patent ownership and invalidity actions for patents/SPCs; INPI and courts share jurisdiction for trademark invalidity since Directive 2015/2436 ('Trademark Package') with specific allocation of grounds between INPI and courts; EUIPO handles EU trademark invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main grounds for patent invalidity: lack of novelty, inventive step, industrial application, added subject‑matter, lack of support in description, insufficient disclosure. Council of State deals with GI invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other methods to remove or limit IP rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Options include declaratory non‑infringement actions, withdrawal/renunciation, exhaustion of rights, and licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaratory non‑infringement can limit enforcement; exhaustion applies when product first put into circulation within EU.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available remedies (interim and final)
rubrics_metrics.description: Main remedies: damages, prohibition (injunction) of further infringement under penalty, destruction of infringing products, order to recall infringing products, communication of information on extent and origin of infringement, publication of judgment or a summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary urgent remedies may be available quickly (even ex parte in some cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of enforcement and costs recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Court fees are generally low; predominant costs are lawyers, bailiff and expert fees; courts may compensate prevailing party for costs in a discretionary amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maximise cost compensation produce justifications of attorney fees invoiced. There is no procedural mechanism enabling or requiring security for costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: COVID‑19 related temporary/procedural changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadlines and court processes were adjusted during the pandemic: deadlines falling between specific dates were extended; INPI extended response deadlines to four months; EUIPO/EPO extended certain deadlines; many hearings postponed or held without hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since May 11, 2020, it was possible to file applications for infringement seizures without hearings; many filings are electronic so filing requirements were largely unaffected.
